paras: The Johnson's box election riot was a deadly clash at the Johnson's polling place in Edgefield County, South Carolina, on election day, November 2, 1880, in which one Black man was killed and several others were wounded. Election-night dispatches blamed Black voters for trying to seize the ballot-box, but evidence in a contested congressional election later said hundreds of Black Republicans had been kept from voting there and that no one had been tried for the killing.

The violence came during the 1880 general election, when an Augusta dispatch reported that the Black vote in the area was the largest in ten years and almost solidly Republican. Edgefield County was expected to return a Democratic majority of several thousand, and specials from the county court house reported that everything had passed off quietly there.

According to a dispatch datelined Augusta, Georgia, a riot broke out at Johnson's between whites and Blacks when "the latter tried to seize the ballot box," leaving one Black man dead and three wounded. Telegrams received at Chester the same day described "a row" at Johnson's box in which one Black man was killed and "several mortally wounded." The Orangeburg Democrat added that the box held a Democratic majority and that the Black men "were repulsed," with three "badly wounded." None of the reports named the dead man, the wounded or any of the whites involved, or said what weapons were used.

No report of an inquest or arrest appears in the coverage. In May 1881 the Burlington Free Press summarized evidence taken in Robert Smalls's contest of G. D. Tillman's election in the Fifth District, which said nearly 500 Black Republicans were "not permitted to exercise the right of suffrage at Johnstone's." The same evidence said a Black man was killed at that polling place and that "the State has made no effort to bring his murderers to trial."

The Augusta dispatch spread widely on November 3 and the following days, appearing in the Chicago Tribune, the St. Paul Daily Globe and many other papers, usually as one item in a column of election returns. South Carolina papers such as the Keowee Courier and the Orangeburg Democrat repeated the ballot-box explanation, and the Orangeburg paper framed the outcome as a successful repulse.

The Republican National Republican in Washington ran the wire under the heading "SOUTH CAROLINA METHODS," mocking it as "Black Sheep Try to Bite White Wolves in Edgefield" with "No Wolves Hurt," and printed thirteen wounded rather than three. A separate Edgefield dispatch of November 4 reported "one negro killed" in an election riot with eleven wounded in one printing and one wounded in another; the Albany, Oregon, State Rights Democrat used it only to accuse the Portland Oregonian of inconsistency about the Southern vote.

The cause of the clash rests on two versions: the election-night wire and the Orangeburg Democrat said Black men tried to seize the ballot-box, while the contested-election evidence printed in 1881 described Black Republicans being kept from voting and called the killers "murderers." The number of wounded also varied, from one to thirteen, with three the figure most often printed; the larger and smaller numbers may be telegraph or typesetting errors.

reader.title: Johnson's box election riot
bases: Whites at the Johnson's polling place on election day killed one Black man and wounded several in what the wire called a riot (A1, A2, A3), and later testimony described Republicans kept from voting there (A23).

The Augusta wire (A1, A2), separate telegrams to Chester (A3), an Edgefield Nov. 4 dispatch (A13, A14) and the 1881 contested-election evidence (A23) agree that one Black man was killed at Johnson's on election day, though they differ on the wounded and on who started it.

framing.detail: The Augusta wire and the Orangeburg Democrat placed the cause on Black voters who 'tried to seize the ballot-box' and 'were repulsed.'
Northern and western papers ran the Augusta wire unchanged in election-news columns.
The National Republican headlined 'SOUTH CAROLINA METHODS' and 'Black Sheep Try to Bite White Wolves in Edgefield-One Sheep Killed and Thirteen Wounded-No Wolves Hurt.'
The Albany State Rights Democrat used the Edgefield dispatch only to attack the Portland Oregonian's consistency on the Southern vote.
The Burlington Free Press, summarizing the contested-election evidence, wrote of 'his murderers' and no effort to try them.

conflicts.note: 'Thirteen' appears in the same wire text that elsewhere reads 'three', and 'eleven'/'one' come from one Edgefield dispatch; these look like telegraph or typesetting variants. 'Three' is the most widely printed figure.
